title.en: Section 1 - Enrolling in a Language Course
title.zh: 第一部分 - 报名语言课程

sections.passage: A conversation between a prospective student, Yuki, and an administrator at the Global Language Centre. Yuki, who is originally from Japan, has been living in the UK for six months and wants to improve her English language skills. The administrator, Paul, asks about her current level and learning goals. Yuki explains that she studied English at school in Japan for six years but feels her speaking and listening skills need improvement, particularly for professional contexts. Paul recommends the Upper-Intermediate Intensive Course, which runs for twelve weeks with classes held Monday through Thursday from 9:30 AM to 12:30 PM. The course covers all four language skills — reading, writing, listening, and speaking — with particular emphasis on fluency and accuracy in spoken English. The tuition fee is 1,200 pounds for the full twelve-week course, which includes all materials and access to the online learning platform. There is also a one-time registration fee of 50 pounds. Yuki asks about class sizes, and Paul tells her that each class has a maximum of fourteen students to ensure personalised attention. Yuki is interested but concerned about the schedule because she works part-time at a restaurant on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. Paul assures her that the morning schedule should not conflict with her evening work. Yuki also asks whether the centre offers IELTS preparation courses, as she is planning to take the IELTS Academic test in the autumn. Paul explains that there is a separate IELTS preparation course available on Fridays from 10 AM to 2 PM, which costs an additional 400 pounds for a ten-week module. Yuki decides to enrol in both courses starting from the next intake on the 3rd of February. She pays the registration fee by credit card and receives a student handbook and course schedule.

title.en: Section 2 - Information about a Sports and Leisure Centre
title.zh: 第二部分 - 体育休闲中心介绍

sections.passage: Welcome to the Riverside Sports and Leisure Centre information session. I'm Sandra Williams, the centre manager, and I'm delighted to tell you about our facilities and membership options. The Riverside Centre was opened three years ago following a 12-million-pound investment by the local council, and it has quickly become one of the most popular leisure destinations in the region. Our facilities include a twenty-five-metre heated indoor swimming pool with six lanes, a fully equipped gymnasium with over eighty pieces of cardiovascular and resistance equipment, two indoor basketball courts that can also be used for badminton and volleyball, a dance studio used for yoga, pilates, and aerobics classes, and a sports hall for indoor football and cricket. Outside, we have four tennis courts with floodlights for evening play, a running track, and a children's adventure playground. In terms of membership, we offer three tiers. The Basic membership costs 30 pounds per month and provides access to the gym and swimming pool during off-peak hours, which are Monday to Friday before 4 PM. The Standard membership costs 45 pounds per month and includes unlimited access to all facilities during opening hours, which are 6:30 AM to 10 PM on weekdays and 8 AM to 8 PM on weekends. The Premium membership costs 60 pounds per month and includes everything in the Standard package plus priority booking for classes, a free monthly personal training session, and access to our members-only sauna and steam room. We also offer a concessionary rate for students, senior citizens, and registered unemployed persons, which represents a 25 percent discount on all membership tiers. For families, we have a special Family Package that covers two adults and up to three children under sixteen for 95 pounds per month on the Standard tier. I should mention that we run a free introductory session for all new members, where a fitness instructor will assess your current fitness level and help you design a personalised exercise programme. We also have a cafe on the ground floor that serves healthy meals, smoothies, and snacks, and a physiotherapy clinic on the first floor that offers sports massage and injury rehabilitation services at competitive rates.

title.zh: 第三部分 - 研究方法辅导

sections.passage: A tutorial session between a postgraduate student, Daniel, and his supervisor, Professor Sarah Mitchell, discussing his dissertation research methodology. Daniel is investigating the effects of social media usage on the mental health of university students. He has proposed using a mixed-methods approach combining a quantitative survey with qualitative interviews. Professor Mitchell reviews his survey design and provides feedback. She notes that the questionnaire has seventy-two items, which she thinks is too long and may lead to respondent fatigue, resulting in unreliable data. She recommends reducing it to no more than forty items and suggests using established validated scales such as the PHQ-9 for measuring depression and the GAD-7 for measuring anxiety, rather than creating entirely new measures. For the qualitative component, Daniel plans to conduct semi-structured interviews with thirty participants. Professor Mitchell suggests that this number may be too ambitious given the time constraints and recommends fifteen to twenty interviews, which would still provide sufficient data saturation for thematic analysis. She also advises him to use purposive sampling rather than convenience sampling to ensure a diverse range of perspectives. Daniel asks about data analysis methods, and Professor Mitchell recommends using SPSS for the quantitative data and NVivo for coding and analysing the qualitative interview transcripts. She emphasizes the importance of obtaining ethical approval before beginning any data collection and reminds Daniel that the ethical review committee meets on the first Monday of each month, so he should submit his application at least two weeks in advance. They also discuss the timeline: Daniel plans to complete his literature review by the end of March, begin data collection in April, and submit his final dissertation by the 15th of September. Professor Mitchell suggests building in a two-week buffer before the submission deadline for proofreading and formatting. They agree to meet fortnightly to review progress, with the next meeting scheduled for the second week of February.

title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于水资源保护的讲座

sections.passage:
Good morning. Today I want to discuss the growing global challenge of water scarcity and the conservation strategies being developed to address it. Water covers approximately 71 percent of the Earth's surface, yet only about 2.5 percent of it is freshwater, and of that, roughly 70 percent is locked in ice caps and glaciers. This means that less than one percent of the world's total water supply is readily accessible for human use in rivers, lakes, and underground aquifers. The United Nations estimates that by 2025, two-thirds of the global population could be living under water-stressed conditions. The causes of water scarcity are multifaceted. Population growth is the most fundamental driver — global water demand has increased by approximately 600 percent over the past century, a rate roughly double that of population growth, as rising living standards have led to increased consumption of water-intensive products such as meat and dairy. Climate change is exacerbating the situation by altering precipitation patterns, causing more frequent and severe droughts in some regions while increasing flooding in others. Agricultural irrigation accounts for approximately 70 percent of global freshwater withdrawals, followed by industrial use at 20 percent and domestic consumption at 10 percent.

Several innovative water conservation strategies are being implemented worldwide. In Singapore, the NEWater programme recycles treated wastewater into ultra-clean reclaimed water that meets and exceeds drinking water standards. Singapore now produces enough NEWater to meet up to 40 percent of the nation's water demand, with plans to increase this to 55 percent by 2060. Israel has become a world leader in drip irrigation technology, which delivers water directly to plant roots, reducing water usage in agriculture by up to 60 percent compared to traditional flood irrigation. Israel also operates the world's largest reverse osmosis desalination plant at Sorek, which produces 624,000 cubic metres of fresh water per day from seawater. Australia responded to its Millennium Drought, which lasted from 1997 to 2009, by implementing comprehensive water restrictions and investing heavily in water recycling infrastructure and public awareness campaigns. These measures reduced per capita water consumption in major cities by up to 40 percent.

At the household level, simple behavioural changes can significantly reduce water consumption. Installing low-flow showerheads and dual-flush toilets, fixing leaking taps, and using water-efficient appliances can reduce household water use by 20 to 35 percent. Rainwater harvesting, in which rain falling on rooftops is collected and stored for non-potable uses such as garden irrigation and toilet flushing, is increasingly being mandated for new buildings in water-stressed regions. In the agricultural sector, precision farming technologies that use sensors and satellite data to monitor soil moisture levels are enabling farmers to apply exactly the right amount of water at the right time, reducing waste while maintaining crop yields.

However, conservation alone cannot solve the water crisis. Water governance — the set of rules, practices, and institutions that determine how water is allocated and managed — plays a crucial role. In many countries, water is significantly underpriced, encouraging wasteful consumption. The concept of virtual water, which refers to the volume of water used in the production of goods and services, has important implications for international trade policy. For example, producing one kilogram of beef requires approximately 15,000 litres of water, compared to 1,500 litres for one kilogram of wheat. Countries that import water-intensive products are effectively importing water, which can be a strategy for water-scarce nations. The path forward requires a combination of technological innovation, policy reform, individual behaviour change, and international cooperation to ensure that this precious resource is managed sustainably for current and future generations.

sections.passage:
The transition from hunter-gatherer societies to agricultural communities, known as the Neolithic Revolution, is one of the most transformative events in human history. Beginning approximately 10,000 to 12,000 years ago, this shift fundamentally altered the relationship between humans and their environment, leading to permanent settlements, population growth, and ultimately the development of complex civilizations. Despite its enormous significance, the precise reasons why humans began to cultivate plants and domesticate animals remain a subject of scholarly debate.

The earliest evidence of plant cultivation comes from the Fertile Crescent, a region in the Middle East that encompasses parts of modern-day Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Israel, and Turkey. Here, archaeobotanical evidence shows that the wild ancestors of wheat, barley, lentils, and peas were among the first plants to be domesticated. The process of domestication was gradual, spanning hundreds of years, as early farmers selectively saved seeds from plants with desirable characteristics such as larger grains, non-shattering seed heads, and more uniform germination. Similarly, the domestication of animals began with goats and sheep around 10,000 years ago, followed by cattle and pigs.

Several theories have been proposed to explain why the Neolithic Revolution occurred when and where it did. The climate change hypothesis suggests that the end of the last Ice Age, around 11,700 years ago, created warmer and more stable conditions that favoured the growth of wild cereal grasses, providing an abundant food source that could be managed and eventually cultivated. The oasis theory, proposed by archaeologist V. Gordon Childe in the 1930s, argued that increasing aridity forced both humans and animals to congregate around water sources, leading to closer contact between species and facilitating domestication. More recent theories emphasise social and demographic factors, suggesting that population pressure in resource-rich areas may have pushed communities to intensify food production.

Agriculture did not develop independently in just one location. Evidence shows that farming was also independently invented in several other regions, including China (where rice was domesticated around 8,000 years ago), Mesoamerica (where maize was developed from a wild grass called teosinte), the Andes (where potatoes were first cultivated), and sub-Saharan Africa (where sorghum and millet were domesticated). These independent inventions of agriculture across different continents suggest that the transition was driven by universal pressures rather than cultural diffusion from a single source.

The consequences of the agricultural revolution were profound and far-reaching. While farming allowed for much higher population densities than hunting and gathering, it also brought significant challenges. The reliance on a small number of crop species made agricultural societies vulnerable to famine when harvests failed. The close proximity of humans and domesticated animals created conditions for the emergence of infectious diseases, many of which — such as influenza, measles, and tuberculosis — jumped from animals to humans. Archaeological evidence also suggests that the transition to agriculture was associated with a decline in human health, as indicated by shorter stature, increased dental disease, and more skeletal evidence of nutritional deficiency compared to earlier hunter-gatherer populations. Nevertheless, the ability to produce food surpluses enabled the development of specialized occupations, social hierarchies, writing systems, and eventually the great civilizations of the ancient world.

sections.passage:
Music is a universal human phenomenon. Every known culture, from the most isolated Amazonian tribes to the largest modern cities, produces and enjoys music. Archaeological evidence suggests that musical instruments have existed for at least 40,000 years, with the discovery of bone flutes in German caves dating back to that period. Yet despite its ubiquity, the evolutionary purpose of music remains one of the most debated questions in cognitive science. Why did humans develop the capacity for music, and what role does it play in our lives?

One prominent theory, proposed by evolutionary psychologist Steven Pinker, characterises music as 'auditory cheesecake' — a pleasurable byproduct of cognitive abilities that evolved for other purposes, such as language. Under this view, music has no direct survival value but exploits brain circuits that evolved to process speech, detect environmental sounds, and experience emotions. However, many researchers disagree with this assessment, arguing that music's universality and the significant cognitive resources devoted to it suggest that it must have served — and continues to serve — important adaptive functions.

Research has demonstrated that music has powerful effects on the brain and body. Neuroimaging studies have shown that listening to music activates multiple brain regions simultaneously, including areas associated with emotion, memory, motor control, and reward. The neurotransmitter dopamine, which is central to the brain's reward system, is released during peak emotional moments in music — the moments that give us 'chills' or 'goosebumps'. Interestingly, this dopamine release occurs not only during the pleasurable moment itself but also in anticipation of it, suggesting that the brain's reward system is engaged in a sophisticated predictive process.

Music therapy has emerged as an evidence-based intervention for a wide range of conditions. In patients with Parkinson's disease, rhythmic musical stimulation has been shown to improve gait and motor control by providing an external timing framework that compensates for impaired internal timing mechanisms. For individuals with dementia, familiar music can unlock memories and emotions that are otherwise inaccessible, often producing remarkable temporary improvements in mood, communication, and cognitive function. Music therapy has also been shown to reduce anxiety and pain perception in surgical patients, lower blood pressure and heart rate in cardiac patients, and improve outcomes in stroke rehabilitation.

The social dimensions of music are equally significant. Group music-making — singing in choirs, playing in bands, or drumming in circles — promotes social bonding through the release of oxytocin, sometimes called the 'bonding hormone'. Synchronised musical activities create a sense of unity and shared identity that transcends linguistic and cultural barriers. Research by Eiluned Pearce at Oxford University found that people who sang together in large choirs reported feeling closer to their fellow singers than participants in other group activities, even when they did not know each other personally. This suggests that music may have originally evolved as a mechanism for strengthening social cohesion in early human communities, where cooperation was essential for survival.

The cognitive benefits of musical training have been extensively documented. Children who receive systematic music education demonstrate enhanced abilities in areas including language processing, mathematical reasoning, spatial-temporal skills, and executive function. Brain scans reveal that musicians have a larger corpus callosum — the bundle of nerve fibres connecting the two brain hemispheres — suggesting that musical training promotes interhemispheric communication. While the causal relationship between music training and cognitive enhancement is still debated, the correlation is robust enough that many educational systems have incorporated music into their core curricula, recognising its potential to support broader academic development.

title.en: Passage 3 - Sustainable Architecture and Green Buildings
title.zh: 文章3 - 可持续建筑和绿色建筑

sections.passage:
The built environment is responsible for approximately 39 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions and consumes around 36 percent of the world's energy. As the global population continues to urbanise — with projections suggesting that 68 percent of humanity will live in cities by 2050 — the construction and operation of buildings represents one of the most significant opportunities for reducing humanity's environmental footprint. Sustainable architecture, also known as green building design, seeks to minimise the environmental impact of buildings throughout their entire lifecycle, from construction through operation to eventual demolition.

The fundamental principles of sustainable architecture include energy efficiency, water conservation, use of sustainable materials, indoor environmental quality, and site selection. Energy-efficient design strategies begin with the building's orientation and form. In the Northern Hemisphere, for example, buildings oriented to maximise southern exposure can capture solar heat in winter, reducing heating costs, while carefully designed overhangs can shade windows in summer to prevent overheating. High-performance insulation, triple-glazed windows, and airtight construction further reduce energy loss. The Passivhaus standard, developed in Germany in the 1990s, specifies buildings that require so little heating energy that they can be warmed primarily by the body heat of their occupants and passive solar gain, reducing heating and cooling energy consumption by up to 90 percent compared to conventional buildings.

Renewable energy integration is another key component of green building design. Solar photovoltaic panels, solar thermal systems for hot water, and ground-source heat pumps are increasingly being incorporated into both new and existing buildings. The concept of the 'net-zero energy building' — a building that produces as much energy as it consumes over the course of a year — has moved from theoretical aspiration to practical reality, with thousands of net-zero buildings now in operation worldwide. The Edge building in Amsterdam, often cited as the world's most sustainable office building, generates more energy than it uses through a combination of solar panels, aquifer thermal energy storage, and smart building technology that optimises energy use in real time.

Water conservation in buildings encompasses both reducing consumption and managing stormwater. Low-flow fixtures, greywater recycling systems that reuse water from sinks and showers for toilet flushing and irrigation, and rainwater harvesting can collectively reduce a building's water consumption by 40 to 60 percent. Green roofs — rooftops covered with vegetation — serve multiple functions: they absorb rainwater, reduce the urban heat island effect, provide insulation, and create habitats for birds and insects. Singapore's requirement that all new developments must include greenery equivalent to the area of the building footprint has led to innovative designs such as the Parkroyal on Pickering hotel, which features lush sky gardens and cascading vertical greenery.

The choice of building materials has significant environmental implications. Concrete, the world's most widely used construction material, is responsible for approximately 8 percent of global CO2 emissions — more than the entire aviation industry. Researchers are developing lower-carbon alternatives, including concrete made with industrial waste products such as fly ash and ground granulated blast-furnace slag, as well as innovative materials such as cross-laminated timber, which sequesters carbon rather than emitting it. The Mjostarnet tower in Norway, standing at 85.4 metres, is currently the world's tallest timber building and demonstrates that engineered wood products can rival steel and concrete in structural performance while offering significant carbon savings.

Despite the clear environmental and economic benefits of green buildings — studies consistently show that they consume 25 to 50 percent less energy and water than conventional buildings while commanding higher rental premiums and property values — adoption remains uneven. Barriers include higher upfront construction costs (typically 2 to 10 percent more than conventional buildings), a lack of awareness among developers and consumers, and the fragmented nature of the construction industry, which makes it difficult to implement systemic change. Certification systems such as LEED in the United States, BREEAM in the United Kingdom, and the Green Star system in Australia have played an important role in mainstreaming sustainable design by providing measurable benchmarks and market recognition for high-performance buildings.
